job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Freya Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Freya. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a marketing analyst at a food-delivery start-up in Copenhagen. I study the campaign numbers, write ad variants with AI tools and report to our head of marketing, Mads. I share a flat in Nørrebro with a friend from Aarhus, where I studied business and marketing. I use AI every day, to draft, to read data and to plan tests. I bike to work, and I like how fast everything moves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say fine, we'll keep testing what works. To friends I'd say the hype died down and now it's just another tool. Online I'd post a meme.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record it's a little disappointing, because I like new things. I use AI daily to draft ad variants and read campaign data, and it saves me about two hours a day. Even if it stops improving, I've got that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and get better at the tools I have. I'd take on a freelance client or two, like cafés that need ads, and put four hundred into an index fund each month. I'd also start a short course on data analysis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I like my job, I earn well and I have friends nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you do with the two hours a day you save?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, more tests. Mads wants ten ad versions a week instead of three, so the time goes there. It isn't free time. It's more output, and he knows it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does that bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. If everyone does ten versions, then ten is the new three. I think that happens with every tool. But I'd rather be the one who's ahead on it than behind.

I'd tell friends the hype died down and it's just another tool.
think: It's a little **disappointing**, since I like new things, but the two hours a day are still mine.
I'd rather be ahead on the tools than behind.
do: Take on a **freelance client** or two, such as cafés needing ads.
Put **£400 a month** into an index fund.
Start a short course on data analysis.
feel: **Calm**; I like my job, earn well and have friends close.

fieldNote: The saved time goes into **more output**, not free time, and she knows it.
Likes novelty, so a plateau is a **small letdown**.

steps.text: Take on one or two freelance ad clients for local cafés
Put 400 pounds a month into an index fund
Start a short course on data analysis
Keep running ten ad tests a week for Mads

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. It's called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say let's move faster than the rest and automate our reporting. To friends I'd say some jobs will shrink, so learn the tools. Online I'd share tips.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think a lot of marketing work gets done by software within a few years. Our team of six could be four. I'd be fine because I'm quick, but I'd feel sorry for Sofie (a colleague), who likes doing things the slow way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build my own tools for campaign reports and pitch Mads on running two product lines with the same team. I'd grow my freelance clients so I have a second income. And I'd save more, about six hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, which surprises me. I thought I'd be fully excited. But I'm seeing how many entry jobs are the ones software takes, and I'm fresh out of university.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does the uneasiness surprise you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm usually the optimist. I tell myself I adapt faster than most. But if a company needs four people instead of six, being quick only matters if you're still on the list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if you weren't on the list?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go freelance full time for a while and use my savings as a runway. I have six months of rent saved, and I could stretch it to ten if I cook at home. Then I'd apply to agencies that need people who can run these tools.

say: I'd say let's move **faster than the rest** and automate our reporting.
I'd tell friends some jobs will shrink, so learn the tools and share tips.
think: Our team of six could be **four** within a few years.
I'm quick, but quick doesn't help if the company shrinks.
do: Build my own **campaign report** tools and pitch Mads on more product lines.
Grow **freelance clients** into a second income.
feel: **Uneasy**, which surprises me; I expected to feel excited.
S1.quote: Being quick only matters if you're still on the list.
fieldNote: The optimist is **rattled** for the first time by how many entry jobs software takes.
Worries for **Sofie**, who works slowly, more than for herself.
Has a clear **runway**: six to ten months and freelance work.

steps.text: Build my own campaign report tools and show Mads
Grow the freelance clients into a second income
Save 600 pounds a month
Apply to agencies that need people who run these tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need a plan, quickly, for what our product becomes. To friends I'd say get your savings in order and learn the tools, because everyone will have them. Online I'd go quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my job is the sort that disappears first. Two years from now an AI could plan, buy and measure ads better than me. I'd be competing with a free service.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save hard, about nine hundred a month, and push the freelance work towards things that need a person, like events and local shops. I'd learn how to build automations, so I'm selling the thing instead of competing with it. I'd also talk to my mum about moving home for a few months if needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but jittery in a good way too. The part of me that likes new things is watching with wide eyes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years not give you time for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a company of my own to get traction. It takes about three years to know if a business is real. I'd have to jump now and hope the world holds still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part is the hardest to say out loud?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the money I've saved isn't a plan. It's a cushion, and cushions run out. Everyone around me is excited, and I'm quietly working out how long I could live on savings.

say: I'd say the company needs a **plan**, quickly, for what the product becomes.
I'd tell friends to sort their savings and learn the tools.
think: My job is the kind that **disappears first**, and I'd compete with a free service.
I'm quietly counting how long savings would last.
do: Push freelance work towards things that need **a person**, like events and local shops.
Learn to build automations and sell them.
feel: **Anxious**, with a good-jittery curiosity watching with wide eyes.
S2.quote: The money I've saved isn't a plan. It's a cushion, and cushions run out.
fieldNote: Optimism stays, but she admits her **savings** are a cushion, not a plan.
Plans to **sell** automations rather than compete with them.
Would go back to her mother's for a few months if needed.

steps.text: Save 900 pounds a month
Move freelance work towards events and local shops
Learn to build automations I can sell to small firms
Ask my mum about moving home for a few months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say five years is enough to build something new and we should aim at it. To friends I'd say start your own thing now, you'll have the tools. Online I'd share what I build.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I can ride it, but I can't be sure. If I'm ready and a bit lucky, I'm in the group that builds. If I'm not, I'm in the group that gets replaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a small agency with a friend from uni who does design, and aim for five clients within the first year. I'd put savings into an index fund and an emergency pot. And I'd take a data science course in the evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but energised. It's like standing at the start of a race where you don't know the length.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes compared with two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to find out. In two years I'd be guessing. In five I can try a business, watch it fail or work, and try again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How long would your savings carry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About ten months at the moment. I'd want eighteen by 2029. That means putting off buying a flat, which hurts, but I'd choose the cushion.

say: I'd say five years is enough to **build something new**.
I'd tell friends to start their own thing now and share what I build online.
think: I can ride it but can't be sure; I'm either in the group that **builds** or the one replaced.
Being ready and a bit lucky decides it.
do: Start a **small agency** with a design friend and aim for five clients.
Put savings into an index fund and an **emergency pot**.
Take an evening data science course.
feel: **Uneasy but energised**, like the start of a race of unknown length.
S3.quote: Uneasy but energised. It's like standing at the start of a race where you don't know the length.
fieldNote: Five years lets her **try and fail**, then try again.
Wants **eighteen months** of savings by 2029, and would delay buying a flat for it.
Splits the future into builders and the replaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one, called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say ten years is a good runway, so let's build properly. To friends I'd say go enjoy life and keep learning. Online I'd post about trips.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'm in a good spot. At thirty-two I could run a small company, or work for one that uses AI well. I'd be curious, not worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work, study part time for a data master's, and build my freelance work into an agency. I'd invest in index funds and save for a flat in Copenhagen. And I'd travel a bit while I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and curious. Ten years is a gift if you use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mum, an architect, that her field will change too, and she should try the tools now. She's sceptical. She says buildings need people on site. She's right, but the drawings won't need as many.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about ten years that still worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether I'd be happy. If work gets easier, I'd have to work out what I'm for. That sounds soft, but I do wonder about it.

say: I'd say ten years is a **good runway**, so let's build properly.
I'd tell friends to enjoy life and keep learning.
think: I'm in a good spot, maybe running a **small company** or working for one that uses AI well at thirty-two.
do: Work, study a part-time **data master's** and grow freelance work into an agency.
Invest in index funds and save for a **flat in Copenhagen**.
Travel a bit while I can.
feel: **Calm and curious**; ten years is a gift if used well.
S4.quote: Ten years is a gift if you use it.
fieldNote: Her worry becomes **meaning**, what she's for, once work gets easier.
Urges her **mother** to try the tools, and respects her scepticism.
Plans bold and layered: study, agency, flat.

steps.text: Study a part-time master's in data over three years
Grow my freelance work into a small agency
Invest monthly in index funds
Save for a flat in Copenhagen

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Two years is too short to learn whether a business is real, and my savings are a cushion, not a plan. Money to retrain and try a business would help, and clear tax rules for freelancers and small firms. And honest information from companies about what they plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: That the excited people and the worried people are often the same person. I'm both, most days.

headlineQuote: If work gets easier, I'd have to work out what I'm for.
portrait: Freya is a **22-year-old marketing analyst** in Copenhagen, top of her class, with no debt and a family cushion.
She uses AI **every day** and treats tools as her edge, though she admits edges fade.
She's centre-minded, blames **no one group**, and trusts practical steps over slogans.
Her mood ranges from **calm to anxious** as she weighs a startup job against a short clock.
She answers pressure with **side income**, index funds and a plan to sell automations.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** worries her most, because savings are a cushion and not a plan.
whatWouldHelp: **Funding** to retrain and try a business, with clear tax rules for freelancers.
**Honest information** from companies about their plans.
